Gram-negative cells appear pink because they lose the crystal violet-iodine complex during decolorization. This happens due to their thin peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane, which allow the dye to be washed away. The remaining cells are stained with safranin, giving them a pink color. This distinction helps identify bacteria as either gram-positive or gram-negative.

Cassava must be processed before it is eaten because it contains cyanogenic glucosides, such as linamarin, which release hydrogen cyanide when the plant tissue is damaged. These compounds are toxic and can cause health issues if consumed without proper processing. Processing, such as grating and roasting, breaks down the cells and reduces the cyanide content, making the cassava safe to eat.

Ṣàlàyé ní èdè Yorùbá ìdí tí a fi gbọ́dọ̀ ṣe ẹ̀gẹ́ (cassava) dáadáa kí a tó jẹ ẹ́. Cassava roots contain cyanogenic glucosides, mainly linamarin, which release hydrogen cyanide when the plant tissue is damaged. Processing reduces this hazard. To make garri, peeled roots are grated, packed into sacks and left to ferment for two to four days while water is pressed out; the mash is then sieved and roasted. Grating breaks the cells so that the enzyme linamarase can act on linamarin, and roasting drives off much of the remaining hydrogen cyanide. Sun-drying of thin chips also lowers cyanide content, but more slowly. For this course, a total cyanide content of 10 mg per kg in the finished flour is the reference safety limit. Poorly processed cassava has been linked to konzo, a paralytic disease, in communities that depend heavily on cassava during food shortages.
